quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Two vowels back to back is awkward to say smoothly. What sound does natural speech add between "three" and "apples" — despite it not appearing in either word's spelling?
quests.explanation: This is a purely phonetic addition: /j/ shows up between "three" and "apples" only to ease pronunciation, with nothing in either word's spelling to account for it.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Check the spelling: "computer" ends in 'r'. Before a consonant or pause it usually stays silent — so what happens before the vowel starting "error"?
quests.explanation: The final 'r' in "computer" behaves like a switch: silent before consonants, audible before vowels. Since "error" starts with a vowel, the /r/ links the two words together smoothly.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "pick" ends in a consonant; "up" begins with a vowel. Try saying them together quickly — which word does that consonant sound like it belongs to now?
quests.explanation: No sound is created or lost here — the final consonant of "pick" simply carries over to open the vowel in "up", which is the essence of linking in connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Nothing in "blue"'s ending suggests a consonant at all. So the /w/ you might hear before "and" isn't really part of either word — where does it come from?
quests.explanation: Vowel hiatus (two vowels in a row) is uncomfortable in fluent English, so an intrusive /w/ fills the gap in "blue and" — a sound created by the flow of speech, not by spelling.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "opera" has no letter for /r/ anywhere at its end. So if you hear a /r/ before "audience", where does it actually come from?
quests.explanation: English avoids putting two vowel sounds directly next to each other, so speakers insert a small linking sound to bridge them. Since "opera" has no /r/ in its spelling, this /r/ is intrusive — added purely for smoothness, not because it's really part of "opera" or "audience".
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The 'r' in "tear" isn't always pronounced. Does the vowel at the start of "it" bring it back to life?
quests.explanation: Because the letter 'r' genuinely exists at the end of "tear", its reappearance before the vowel in "it" is called linking /r/ — a real, spelled sound resurfacing, unlike intrusive /r/, which comes from nowhere in the spelling.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a classic resyllabification moment. What happens to the last sound of "plug" once the vowel of "it" is right there waiting?
quests.explanation: Because a vowel immediately follows, the closing consonant of "plug" doesn't stay put — it links forward into "it", exactly as fluent speakers naturally do.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a sound-merging boundary. What new consonant replaces /s/ + /j/ when you say "this yoga" naturally?
quests.explanation: Coalescence is a genuine sound change, not just fast talking — /s/ plus /j/ reliably becomes /ʃ/ in phrases like "this yoga" across natural English speech.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This 'r' is real — it's written into "doctor" — but often silent. Listen for it specifically at the boundary with "in".
quests.explanation: Speakers keep the /r/ silent in "doctor" only until a vowel gives it a reason to surface. "in" provides exactly that vowel, so the /r/ links the phrase together.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Unlike a sound added from nowhere, the /r/ here is already part of "winter"'s spelling. What triggers it to reappear before "is"?
quests.explanation: This linking /r/ is predictable from spelling alone: any r-final word behaves this way before a vowel, and "winter is" is a clean example of it.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try blending "fit" straight into "your" without a pause. The /t/ and /j/ fuse — into what sound?
quests.explanation: The two sounds don't just sit next to each other; they blend into /tʃ/. That's the defining feature of coalescence, and it's exactly what happens in "fit your".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say the phrase at normal speed. Does the final consonant of "fill" stay cleanly inside "fill", or does it glide forward into "it"?
quests.explanation: This kind of linking happens constantly in natural English: a final consonant reaches across the word boundary to join the next vowel, connecting "fill" and "it" into one flowing phrase.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen closely at the boundary of "project" and "deadline" — count the consonants stacking up. Does the /t/ still make it into the sentence?
quests.explanation: In fast, connected speech, a /t/ wedged between consonants almost always disappears. That's what you'll hear in "project deadline" — the /t/ goes silent.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "send" ends in a clear consonant sound, and "it" starts with a vowel. What happens to that consonant when you say them together naturally?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in a consonant meets a word starting with a vowel, the consonant shifts to open the next syllable instead of closing the first. In "send it", the final consonant of "send" links smoothly onto the vowel that begins "it".
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "need" ends in /d/ and "your" begins with a /j/ sound. What single new consonant do the two combine into?
quests.explanation: When /d/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two often fuse into a single new consonant. In "need your", /d/ + /j/ becomes /dʒ/ — a completely different sound from either original.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the consonant joining "could" to "buy". Is it still /d/, or has it changed shape to match what follows?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in /d/ meets a bilabial sound, the /d/ shifts to /b/ so both sounds are made in nearly the same place in the mouth. That's what happens in "could buy".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "kept calm" naturally, without pausing between the words. Is the /t/ audible, or does it disappear into the next consonant?
quests.explanation: Elision removes a sound completely rather than merely blending it. Here the /t/ vanishes from "kept" so the phrase moves directly into "calm".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This pair, "spend less", creates a tricky consonant sequence. Which sound do fluent speakers simplify away — and is it really gone, or just quieter?
quests.explanation: Speakers naturally avoid three consonants in a row, so the /d/ is dropped rather than forced through. That's why "spend less" sounds smoother without it.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "over" ends in a silent 'r' on its own. Say it together with "and" — does that silence hold, or break?
quests.explanation: Because "over" ends in 'r', the connected-speech rule is simple: pronounce the /r/ whenever a vowel follows, as it does before "and". That's what makes this linking rather than intrusion.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "show off" as one smooth unit, not two separate words. Where does the final consonant of "show" end up?
quests.explanation: This is linking: the consonant isn't added, dropped, or changed — it simply moves to attach to the following vowel. That's exactly what happens between "show" and "off".
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Fluent speech avoids awkward consonant pile-ups. Where exactly does that simplification happen in "protect data"?
quests.explanation: This cluster is simplified by deleting the /t/ altogether — not weakening it, not shifting it, just leaving it out — which is the defining feature of elision in "protect data".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The consonant at the end of "save" has a vowel waiting right after it in "it". Does it stay attached to "save", or slide onto the next syllable?
quests.explanation: Fluent English resyllabifies across word boundaries whenever a consonant meets a vowel. Here, the last sound of "save" glides directly into "it", making the phrase sound like one continuous unit.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Because "manager" is spelled with a final 'r', a vowel right after it — like the one starting "is" — can bring that /r/ back into speech. Listen for it.
quests.explanation: The /r/ you hear between "manager" and "is" isn't invented — it's the word's own final letter reactivated by the vowel that follows, which is the textbook definition of linking /r/.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Both "Russia" and "and" end and begin with vowel sounds. Listen for an extra consonant sound that sneaks in between them.
quests.explanation: This is intrusion: a sound appears between two vowels even though it isn't written anywhere. In "Russia and", an intrusive /r/ bridges the gap, purely to avoid an awkward vowel collision.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In connected speech, the /t/ ending "net" often adapts to its neighbor. What does it turn into right before the bilabial sound in "profit"?
quests.explanation: This is place assimilation: /t/ moves to a bilabial position to blend smoothly with what comes next, turning into /p/ in "net profit".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Instead of hearing /z/ and /j/ separately between "close" and "your", listen for one fused sound. What is it?
quests.explanation: This is coalescent assimilation: two adjacent sounds merge into a third sound that resembles neither one alone. Here, /z/ and /j/ combine into /ʒ/ in "close your".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "here" already has a written 'r' at the end — normally silent before a pause, but what happens to it right before the vowel that opens "is"?
quests.explanation: "here" ends in a written 'r' that's silent in isolation (in non-rhotic pronunciation) but reappears whenever a vowel follows. Because "is" begins with a vowel, the /r/ resurfaces — this is linking /r/, not intrusion, since the letter is genuinely there in "here".
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "flu epidemic" without a pause. Two vowel sounds are about to collide — what does English insert to smooth the transition?
quests.explanation: Because "flu" ends in a vowel and "epidemic" begins with one, English speakers instinctively insert /w/ between them. It's not in the spelling of either word — it's added on the fly to keep the speech flowing.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "fast" alone, then "food" alone — both consonants are clear. Now blend them at speed. What happens to the /t/ in between?
quests.explanation: Notice that nothing replaces the /t/ — it isn't weakened or swapped for another sound, it's simply omitted. That full deletion is what separates elision from assimilation in "fast food".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "phase your" quickly and casually. The /z/ and the /j/ in "your" don't stay separate — what do they merge into?
quests.explanation: Rather than two separate consonants, connected speech blends /z/ and /j/ into /ʒ/. That's why "phase your" sounds like one smooth unit rather than two words bumping together.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.
